lines.text: The snow left Greyhollow early that year. By the first week of spring, the whole north had decided it deserved a festival, and nobody could think why not.
So we held the first Thaw Festival in Greyhollow's history. Tobin built a bonfire the size of a house. Pell sold everything that wasn't nailed down, and two things that were.
Festival ribbons! Blessed by the Lord of the North himself!
I haven't blessed anything, Pell.
You walked past the box, my lord. It counts.
Halvard danced with Granny, and lost. Ysolde danced with Corvin, and they argued about the price of the musicians the whole time.
Maric asked Wren to dance. Wren looked at me and asked if she could shoot him.
You have a problem, Wren.
My father and Bram sat together by the fire all evening: two old men who had kept the same secret for fifteen years, and had nothing left to keep. They didn't need to talk.
And then Oswin climbed up onto a barrel.
Sir Oswin Hale, who had been drunk for ten years and sober for two, and had never once sung in front of anybody.
This one's for the ones we lost. And for Dunn. Sing it if you know it. Shout it if you don't.
He sang an old soldiers' song about coming home in spring. His voice was terrible. Nobody cared. By the second verse the whole north was singing.
Nell fell asleep on Ash halfway through. Ash didn't move for three hours. He wouldn't have moved for an army.
Late that night, I took Bram's key and went to the walled garden.
I had dug it over myself in the last of the snow, and cut back the dead wood. Claimed it, I suppose, the only way I know. By looking after it.
The roses were out. Red and white, in the moonlight, for the first time in fifteen years.
She'd be glad, my lord.
I'm going to bring her home, Bram. Whatever it costs.
I know. That's what frightens me.
The war had lasted one winter. We had won every fight that mattered, and lost people I'll never stop counting. I thought the worst was behind us.
At dawn, a rider came up the south road in Varr colours, grey with dust and swaying in the saddle.
My lords. There's a fever in the midlands. Whole villages are down with it. Thousands sick, and the Order is only curing the loyal houses.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter one hundred and thirty-five, coming soon.
